lesson.title: Stepwise Refinement: From Rough Plan to Working Code
lesson.summary: Demonstrates how to develop a solution gradually, starting from a vague, high level plan and refining it in stages into precise, runnable Python code, building on decomposition.
lesson.body:
Decomposition tells you to break a problem into smaller pieces. Stepwise refinement tells you what to do once those pieces still feel too vague to code directly: refine them, gradually, in stages, until each one is precise enough to translate directly into a programming language. Rather than jumping from "I have an idea" straight to finished code, stepwise refinement moves through a series of increasingly detailed descriptions, each one closer to something a computer can execute. This matters because jumping straight from a vague idea to finished code is exactly where beginners get stuck: there are too many decisions to make all at once, and stepwise refinement spreads those decisions out over several manageable passes instead.

Consider the task of writing a program that warns a user if the temperature is dangerously high. A first, very rough plan might simply say: "get the temperature, decide if it's dangerous, tell the user." That is not code, it is barely even a plan, but it captures the shape of the solution. The next refinement adds detail to each piece: "ask the user to enter a temperature as a number. If that number is above 100, print a warning message. Otherwise, print that conditions are normal." This version is closer to code because each phrase maps almost directly onto a Python construct: input, a comparison, and a print statement.

The final refinement turns that description into working Python:

temperature = float(input("Enter the temperature: "))
if temperature > 100:
    print("Warning: dangerously high temperature")
else:
    print("Conditions are normal")

Trace this with an entered value of 104. input() reads the text "104" as a string, and float() converts it into the number 104.0. The condition temperature > 100 evaluates to True, since 104.0 is greater than 100, so the program prints the warning message and skips the else branch entirely. If the user had entered 85, float() would produce 85.0, the condition would be False, and the program would print that conditions are normal instead. Each refinement stage did not change what the program was trying to do, it only added precision, until the description was unambiguous enough for Python to execute directly.

Stepwise refinement is valuable because it lets you postpone hard decisions instead of getting stuck on them immediately. In the rough plan, you do not yet need to know whether the threshold should be 100 or 90, or whether the input comes from a sensor or a keyboard. You can make those decisions during a later refinement, once the overall shape of the solution is already settled. This mirrors how real software gets built: broad strokes first, sharpened gradually, rather than attempting to write perfect, final code in a single pass. Writers use the same approach when they draft an outline before a full essay, and architects use it when they sketch a floor plan before specifying which screws hold the cabinets in place.
